notes.meaning: Paul asks if he seems to be bragging about himself again. False teachers in Corinth carried written letters of recommendation from other places to win trust. Paul did not need letters of introduction to a church that he had founded himself.

The Corinthian believers were Paul's real letter of recommendation. Their turn to faith was held deeply in his heart and could be observed by everyone. A changed Christian life is like an open book that the whole world can read.

Christ wrote this living letter through Paul's preaching. It was not written with ordinary ink or carved on stone slabs like the Ten Commandments given to Moses. Instead, the Holy Spirit carved it onto soft human hearts that were changed and renewed by God's grace.
Paul expresses a firm confidence about the fruit of his work. This bold trust did not come from human pride or personal talent. It came entirely through Christ and looked toward God for help.

No worker for God has the ability to carry out this ministry by human strength alone. On our own, we cannot even think a good thought or change a single human heart. All our ability and fitness come from God as a gift.

God made the apostles fit to serve a new covenant, which is God's new promise of life through Christ. They do not minister an outward written code, which only condemns lawbreakers to death. Instead, they minister the Holy Spirit, who brings true life to the soul.

differ.view: The law only demands what sinners cannot perform, so preaching the law brings death while only the gospel gives life and righteousness.
The law is called a killing letter because it reveals our spiritual illness without providing a cure, but it kills only because human nature is corrupt.
The killing effect of the law comes from human sinfulness rather than any flaw in the law itself, and believers are now enabled by the Spirit to obey God's commands.

notes.meaning: The old law carved on stones brought a sentence of death, yet it arrived with great brightness. When Moses received it on Mount Sinai, his face shone with such light that the Israelites were afraid to look at him. Even though that shining light was temporary and faded away, it showed the holiness of God's law.

Paul reasons from the smaller thing to the greater. If a ministry that brought death was accompanied by bright glory, the ministry of the Holy Spirit must be far more glorious. The gospel brings eternal life to people, which is far greater than outward flashes of light on a mountain.

The law brought condemnation, which is God's guilty verdict against sinners. In contrast, the gospel brings righteousness, meaning God forgives believers and accepts them through faith in Jesus. A message that saves and justifies lost people holds far more glory than a law that only points out their guilt.

The glory of the old law seems like nothing when compared to the greater glory of the gospel. Just as the bright light of the morning sun makes the moon and stars fade from view, the coming of Christ outshines the old system. The grace of Jesus reveals God's majesty far more clearly.

The old covenant was meant to last only for a season until Christ came. In contrast, the new covenant will stand forever and never pass away. What lasts through eternity has a far higher and deeper glory than something that only lasted for a short time.

Ministers of the gospel have great confidence because their message rests on an everlasting promise. Because their hope is so sure, they speak openly and plainly without hiding anything. They do not wrap the truth in riddles or confusing shadows.

Moses placed a cloth veil over his face after speaking with God so the Israelites would not gaze at the fading glow. That covering was also a symbol showing that the people could not see the final purpose of that temporary law. Christian teachers do not wear a veil because they openly declare Christ, who is the true goal of the law.

The minds of the people became hardened and dull toward God's message. Even in Paul's time, whenever the old covenant scriptures were read, an invisible veil still hid their true meaning. That veil can be taken away only through personal faith in Christ.

Whenever the books of Moses were read aloud in the synagogues, a spiritual veil lay over the people's hearts. They heard the outward words, but their minds remained closed to the spiritual truth. They could not see that their own scriptures pointed straight to Jesus.

Whenever someone turns to the Lord in faith, that blindfold is taken away. When Moses turned back to talk with God, he took off his veil, and sinners experience the same when they turn to Christ. The shadows vanish, and the true meaning of God's Word becomes clear.

The Lord works through his Holy Spirit to give life to his Word. Wherever the Spirit of the Lord is present, believers receive true freedom. This means freedom from the curse of sin, freedom from fear, and open access to God's presence.

differ.view: Christ is called the Spirit here because he is the true soul and life of the law, turning what would be a dead letter into living truth.
The passage directly identifies the person of the Holy Spirit as the Lord who brings supernatural freedom and direct access to God.

notes.meaning: All believers look upon the glory of the Lord with open, unveiled faces, as though seeing him in the mirror of the gospel. As we keep our eyes on Christ, the Holy Spirit steadily changes our character to match his likeness. This work transforms us with an ever-increasing glory that comes from God.

differ.view: The phrase from glory to glory can mean that the Christian journey starts in glory and finds its final goal in glory, rather than just step-by-step progress.
Some read the words as pointing to the beginning and final end of our transformation in Christ, while others see it as gradual growth in holiness.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: This verse describes deification, the lifelong process where believers are healed of sinful passions and transformed into living icons of Christ's likeness.
